extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, policymakers, and stakeholders in the patent community (industry, academia, inventors, and associations)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate standards for determining patent eligible subject matter under U.S. law (35 U.S.C. §101), including the Supreme Court’s Mayo/Alice two-step test, historical doctrine, Federal Circuit application, technology‑specific impacts (life sciences and computer-related), and public/legislative recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis: 35 U.S.C. § 101 (eligible categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory language establishes the basic categories of patent-eligible subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and requires usefulness; eligibility is the threshold requirement but an invention must also satisfy §§102, 103, and 112 (novelty, non-obviousness, written description/enablement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicially-created exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have long carved out exceptions to patent eligibility for laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These judicial exceptions (e.g., principle-in-the-abstract, natural products, abstract ideas) operate as limits on §101 even though the statutory text lists broad categories; many modern disputes center on the scope and application of these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, determine whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by the Supreme Court in Mayo and Alice; used by courts and the USPTO to decide eligibility. Examples: Mayo found claims to a drug‑metabolite relationship ineligible under the two-step test; Alice found mere computer implementation of an abstract idea insufficient at step two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (useful clue, not sole test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim is more likely eligible if it is tied to a particular machine or apparatus, or if it transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court (Bilski) described the machine-or-transformation test as 'a useful and important clue' but rejected it as the exclusive test for process eligibility. Use as a strong indicium but do not treat as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern as limiting principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A key rationale for the judicial exceptions is to prevent patents from preempting all practical applications of a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether claims would 'pre-empt' use of the underlying principle; critics argue preemption analysis collapses §101 into §§102/103/112 and is sometimes applied inconsistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics for natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: A naturally occurring product that has been altered to have 'markedly different characteristics from any found in nature' may be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty and related precedent: inventions that create organisms or molecules with new characteristics (e.g., engineered bacterium, cDNA in Myriad) can be eligible because they are not merely products of nature; the absence of chemical change or merely isolating native genes can render claims ineligible (Myriad’s isolated genomic DNA held ineligible; cDNA held eligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere recitation of conventional or routine steps is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that add only well-understood, routine, conventional steps to a law of nature or natural phenomenon do not supply the inventive concept required under step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Mayo and Ariosa (Sequenom): claims that 'begin and end' with a natural phenomenon and insert conventional laboratory steps have been found ineligible. Examiners and courts scrutinize whether additional steps are novel and inventive versus routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be 'directed to' an application, not merely to an abstract principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis asks what the claim is 'directed to'—the invention’s focus—so claims directed to a practical application (a new technique, treatment, or transformation) are more likely eligible than claims directed to an abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit cases (e.g., the cryopreservation decision) emphasize evaluating the claim’s directedness: identify whether the patent is claiming a new laboratory technique or merely the natural ability/relationship itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer or reciting generic computer components does not transform the idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice: 'mere recitation of a generic computer' fails to supply an inventive concept at step two. Claims should include specific, non-conventional computer improvements or novel technical solutions to be persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process as transformation (Cochrane definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is 'an act, or a series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing,' provided it is new and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical definition supports eligibility for processes that effect a physical transformation; it is a relevant factor when assessing manufacturing and treatment claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas and algorithms require inventive application
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical formulas, scientific truths, and algorithms are not patentable in the abstract; to be eligible they must be applied in a novel and useful structure or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gottschalk v. Benson and Parker v. Flook: claiming a mathematical algorithm alone (or with known post-solution activity) risks ineligibility unless the claim integrates the algorithm into a novel, practical application or technical process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim 'as a whole'; avoid improper dissection
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be considered in their entirety; courts warn against dissecting claims into old and new elements and ignoring the old elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr cautioned that parsing claims to isolate a judicial exception while ignoring the overall combination can be inappropriate; the ordered combination may supply eligibility even if individual elements appear conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate eligibility inquiry from §§102/103/112 patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility under §101 is conceptually distinct from novelty (§102), non-obviousness (§103), and written description/enablement/definiteness (§112), though overlap and practical interplay exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters and legislative proposals urge clearer separation so that issues of scope, novelty, and enablement are addressed under their respective provisions rather than folded into §101 determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application / useful arts test (proposed alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some public and legislative proposals recommend replacing the Mayo/Alice framework with a 'technological' or 'useful arts' test that treats claims as eligible if they contribute to the technological arts or recite a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals vary: some would expressly permit claims that recite a practical application of a law/phenomenon/idea while preventing claims that preempt all applications; proponents argue this aligns U.S. law with international norms and reduces unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that 'begin and end' with a natural phenomenon (diagnostic claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic claims that start with the detection of a natural phenomenon and end with its recognition are vulnerable to ineligibility absent inventive additional steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequenom/Ariosa: courts found methods that merely detect natural biomarkers and apply routine techniques to analyze them to be ineligible; adding novel, unconventional steps or restrictive applications can alter the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overbreadth is often better addressed under §§112 or 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Some judges and commentators argue that claims that are overly broad should be policed under disclosure (§112) or obviousness (§103) rather than by broadly applying §101 exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view suggests using stricter claim construction, definiteness and enablement review, or obviousness analysis to limit overbroad claims instead of deeming subject matter ineligible at the threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-specific considerations (life sciences vs. computer-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of §101 principles varies by technology domain: life sciences cases often turn on whether claimed materials/diagnostics are natural products or merely isolated natural phenomena, while computer-related cases focus on abstract ideas implemented on computers and whether inventive technical improvements are claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report documents differential Federal Circuit outcomes: life sciences decisions emphasize natural-product and natural-phenomenon issues (e.g., Myriad, Ariosa), whereas computer cases emphasize abstract ideas and generic computer implementation (Alice). Examiners and drafters should tailor claims and arguments to technology-specific precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of definitional statutory language in legislative proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Various public proposals include explicit statutory definitions (e.g., defining 'law of nature', 'natural product', 'abstract idea') and procedural rules (e.g., 'sole exception', or that eligibility be determined 'without regard' to §§102/103/112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the appendix: IPO/AIPLA/NYIPLA/HIPLA proposals—some propose that a claim is ineligible only if it 'exists in nature independently of and prior to any human activity' or that 'abstract idea' excludes processes performed by computer programs. These definitions would materially alter eligibility analyses if enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative responses and USPTO examination guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO examination guidance and training materials interpret and apply Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent in examination practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO convened roundtables and issued guidance following the Supreme Court decisions; administrative measures (guidance, examiner training, examples) are a recommended path for addressing eligibility issues short of legislative change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies to mitigate preemption concerns: research exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: One public recommendation is to establish a research exemption to infringement to alleviate concerns that broad eligibility exclusions were motivated by fear of preemption of research and downstream innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A targeted research exemption (limited experimentation to understand or improve patented subject matter) was proposed to reduce chilling effects on basic research without eroding patent rights generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: International consistency and TRIPS considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility approaches should be considered in light of international agreements (TRIPS) and practices of other major patent offices (Europe, Japan, Korea, China) which may differ in how they treat natural products, diagnostics, software, and business methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report reviews international approaches and notes policy arguments about harmonizing U.S. law with internationally accepted norms to reduce fragmentation and uncertainty for global innovators.
